c0615: PHASE 1: BUSINESS SETUP & TAXES (18-12 months before opening)
c0620: Choose your legal structure: LLC vs S corp
c0623: The financial plan assumes an effective income tax rate of 25% (21% federal as a C corporation plus state). An LLC taxed as a pass-through pays through your personal return instead, and early losses carry forward as net operating losses. Compare the options with your CPA using the plan's numbers.
c0624: Form the LLC before you sign the lease
c0627: The lease, the zoning application and the permits all go in the LLC's name, so form it first. Ask your CPA how much capital to put in.
c0628: Get your EIN (IRS) and register the LLC with your state
c0630: The EIN is free from the IRS. The venue and your exclusive caterer are separate businesses, each with its own EIN. Register the LLC with your Secretary of State and keep the annual report date on your calendar.
c0632: Open your state withholding and unemployment insurance accounts before your first hire. Decide with your CPA how you will pay yourself (owner's draw vs salary), based on your tax election.
c0633: Business license and sales tax permit
c0635: Ask your state whether your venue rental fee is taxable and, if it is, register for a sales tax permit. Check the city and county business license too.
c0637: Keep it separate from your personal accounts: couples' retainers, the caterer commission and the rent all run through it.
c0640: Set up payroll for your seasonal W-2 staff. Give a receipt or invoice for every payment, retainers included. Choose venue management software (Tripleseat, Perfect Venue, HoneyBook) that tracks retainers, scheduled payments and the caterer commission.
c0641: Sales tax returns (quarterly filer in the plan)
c0643: The plan uses one example sales tax rate on the venue rental fee and services, and 0% on the caterer commission. The caterer bills the menu and the bar to the couple and handles its own tax. Ask your state about your filing calendar (monthly, quarterly or annual) and whether the site fee is taxable.
c0644: Estimated taxes and owner's draw plan
c0646: Set up quarterly estimated tax payments with your CPA and agree how you will pay yourself (draw vs salary), depending on whether the LLC is taxed as a pass-through or as a corporation.
c0647: Lender package: the plan plus two SBA 7(a) quotes
c0648: Bring the full plan with the month-by-month cash flow. The lease, counting renewal options, should run at least as long as the loan: SBA lenders typically require this; confirm with your lender. You don't own the property: ask what collateral they accept.
c0649: USPTO trademark search for the venue name
c0650: Search the name before you print anything: check the federal database for event venue and wedding services, your state's business name records and the domain name.
c0653: Privacy policy, terms of service and the consent language for your quote forms. Get written permission to use photos of couples and events.
c0656: Use the dropdown: ✓, ☐, N/A. ✓ = done, ☐ = pending, N/A = not applicable and comes out of the total.
c0658: PHASE 2: ZONING & PERMITS (18-6 months before opening)
c0659: Zoning check in writing before signing anything
c0662: Ask the county planning office IN WRITING whether a wedding or event venue is allowed on that parcel and under which permit (conditional use permit or special use permit). A verbal answer is not a permit. Ask about the zoning district, any overlays and whether agritourism rules apply.
c0663: Choose a property with an existing barn or building, 30-60 minutes from the city
c0665: A hall, restrooms and a kitchen area that already exist save build-out cost and permitting time. The plan targets a property 30-60 minutes from a mid-size or larger city. Confirm what the zoning allows before falling in love with a barn.
c0668: Have an engineer check the available electrical capacity, whether the water comes from a public system or a well (if a well will serve your guests, ask your state drinking water program), and whether the septic system can handle your guest count.
c0669: Negotiate the lease: long term, counting renewal options
c0672: The build-out goes on land you don't own, so the term, counting renewal options that only you can exercise, should be at least as long as your loan: SBA lenders typically require this; confirm with your lender. Aim for a term long enough to recover your investment.
c0673: Lease contingent on CUP approval (and the certificate of occupancy)
c0676: The lease should not bind you if the conditional use permit or the certificate of occupancy is denied. Negotiate a rent-free or reduced-rent period while you build and get permits.
c0677: Purchase option or right of first refusal, landlord consent and TI allowance
c0678: Ask for a purchase option or a right of first refusal if the landlord sells. Get the landlord's written consent to the build-out and to using the lease as collateral for your loan, and negotiate a tenant improvement (TI) allowance. If the property is family-owned, the rent should still be at market: check with your CPA.
c0679: Apply for the conditional / special use permit (CUP / SUP)
c0682: Expect a public hearing. The county may attach conditions such as a cap on events, hours, traffic and noise. Timelines vary by county: ask the planning office. Your lease should depend on the outcome.
c0683: Change of occupancy to assembly (Group A-2): building permit to certificate of occupancy
c0684: Turning a barn into a place of assembly usually means a building permit and a certificate of occupancy for assembly use (Group A-2). Ask the building official what the change requires for your building, and don't assume an older building is exempt.
c0685: Ask the building official and the fire marshal in writing
c0686: Ask about occupant load, sprinklers, exits, restrooms and tents, and keep the answers. They set the maximum guest count you can book and drive the cost of the build-out. Rules differ by state, county and city.
c0687: No firm dates without the CUP and the certificate of occupancy
c0689: If the permit is denied or delayed, you will have to refund what you collected. Before the permits arrive, accept only contingent holds with a full refund if they don't, agreed in writing (clause 2A of the contract template, Contingent booking before permits). Once you hold the permits, they become firm bookings.
c0690: ADA Title III: accessible routes, restrooms and parking
c0692: A venue you rent to the public is a place of public accommodation. Put accessible routes, restrooms and parking on the plans from the first drawing (2010 ADA Standards) and confirm the details with your architect.
c0693: Occupant load, exits and emergency plan
c0695: The fire marshal sets the maximum occupancy. Post the occupant load, keep exits clear and marked, install emergency lighting and write an evacuation plan. Tents have their own fire-code rules, so ask the fire marshal. Never book more guests than your certificate of occupancy allows. Your county or city may ask for more.
c0696: Noise: county ordinance, decibel limit and sound meter
c0697: Many county ordinances limit amplified sound, usually with a lower limit at night. Ask the county for the limit that applies to your property. A sound meter with a log is your proof if a neighbor complains.
c0698: Outdoor music and curfew under the CUP
c0700: The CUP conditions and the county ordinance set the curfew. Ask, and write it into your contract with the couple. If you allow music, make sure ASCAP, BMI and SESAC licensing is covered.
c0701: Insurance: general liability, host liquor liability, property and umbrella
c0704: Get quotes from an agent who insures venues. Lenders, landlords and your caterer will ask for certificates of insurance (COI). Add coverage for damage to improvements and for loss of income. Costs vary by state and guest count: get local quotes.
c0708: If a well serves your guests, it may count as a public water system. Ask your state drinking water program about testing and permitting before the first event, and don't assume private-well rules apply.
c0710: PHASE 3: BUILD-OUT & EQUIPMENT (12-3 months before opening)
c0711: Three bids based on the architect's plans
c0713: Compare them line by line with the "Startup Costs" sheet of the financial plan.
c0714: Building permit before the work starts
c0716: Ask your county or city building department which permits the work needs, and don't start without them.
c0717: Barn renovation: floors, doors, insulation, finishes
c0720: Floors, doors and windows, insulation and finishes on the existing building.
c0721: Ask the fire marshal in writing whether you need sprinklers and an alarm. Cost depends on your water supply and local code: get local quotes.
c0722: ADA-compliant restrooms (and septic expansion if needed)
c0723: Accessible route to the hall, the tent and the restrooms: check it with your architect. Include any septic expansion here.
c0724: Electrical service, exit and emergency lighting, with inspection
c0727: Panel, exterior and emergency lighting, and power for the hall, the tent and the caterer's kitchen.
c0728: Size it for the hall and the prep & warming kitchen. Service it before each season.
c0729: Heating and cooling: the hall is used all year, including August.
c0730: Caterer's prep & warming kitchen with water and drain
c0732: Design it with the exclusive caterer you plan to sign: walk-in cooler, sinks, stainless steel tables and a plating area. This is a support kitchen, not a production kitchen. Ask your county whether it needs a health plan review.
c0736: This is your rain plan. Check the local fire code for tent permits and ask the manufacturer for the installation and wind-load documentation.
c0737: 200 chairs, tables, base linens and bridal suite
c0738: Tables, 200 chairs and base linens. The couples hire any special decor. Furnish the bridal suite and the groom's lounge.
c0740: A meter that logs its readings is your evidence if a neighbor files a noise complaint.
c0741: Gravel parking, driveway, signage and lighting (ADA spaces)
c0743: Plan about one parking space for every 2.5-3 guests (Kit estimate), a driveway that holds up in the rain, lighting and accessible spaces.
c0746: Plant early: the garden in your photos takes a season to look good.
c0747: Final inspections and certificate of occupancy
c0750: Fire marshal and building inspections, extinguishers, exit signs and emergency lighting, and the certificate of occupancy that lets you open.
c0752: PHASE 4: STAFF & EXCLUSIVE CATERER (6-2 months before opening)
c0753: Hire the venue coordinator as a seasonal W-2 employee
c0755: Offer letter, I-9 and W-4, with the season (March to November) in writing. From December to February the owner coordinates.
c0756: Event attendants as seasonal part-time W-2 staff
c0758: Never as 1099 contractors who invoice you: if you direct their schedule and their work, they would be misclassified. For peaks, use a staffing agency.
c0759: Facilities & grounds, weekend sales and housekeeping
c0760: Part-time positions with the hours in the plan. Pay at least the higher of the federal and state minimum wage (check your local one too), and confirm with your CPA.
c0761: Workers' comp and state new-hire reporting before each season
c0763: Confirm your state's rules for ending seasonal employment when the season closes.
c0766: Required for all staff, including events that run late. Overtime applies above 40 hours a week (FLSA).
c0767: Basic safety: OSHA, first aid, ladders and loads
c0770: A safety plan for setup, lifting, working at height, grounds work and driving on the property.
c0771: Shortlist one or two exclusive caterers and hold a tasting
c0773: A tasting with each, references from other venues, the health permit for their kitchen and their insurance. The exclusive caterer is half your venue's reputation.
c0776: Exclusivity and term, hours, cleaning of the prep & warming kitchen, exit and penalties. Use the Exclusive Caterer Agreement template in this pack.
c0777: Monthly commission statement and audit right
c0779: The plan assumes a caterer commission of 10% of the F&B sales the caterer makes at your venue. It is an assumption, so negotiate it. Make each event's guest count verifiable.
c0780: Caterer's food safety plan and incident contact
c0782: Ask for the caterer's food safety plan: temperature control, a Certified Food Protection Manager on site and food handler cards for staff. Get a contact for incidents and keep a copy on file.
c0783: Allergens for each menu in writing
c0784: The caterer handles the 9 major food allergens: ask for the allergen information for each dish in writing and collect the guests' allergies with the final headcount, for every event.
c0785: Caterer's health permit, liquor license and COI
c0786: The caterer holds the health permit for the kitchen it uses and its own liquor license or permit. The venue holds neither. Ask for a COI naming the venue as additional insured, including liquor liability.
c0789: Photographers, music, florists and decor that know the venue, each with a COI. Decide whether to charge an outside vendors fee when couples bring their own, and put it in the contract.
c0791: PHASE 5: BRAND, PRICING & BOOKINGS (12-3 months before opening)
c0792: Venue name, logo and brand identity
c0793: Do it before the website and the wedding marketplaces: it's what couples will see when they compare.
c0794: Website with availability, gallery and venue tour booking
c0795: Real photos of the venue set up, guest capacity, event types and how to book a tour.
c0796: Styled shoot: professional photos and video of the venue set up
c0798: As soon as the build-out is done
c0799: Set a real wedding table with the caterer for the photos. Without photos there are no bookings.
c0800: Google Business Profile and first reviews
c0801: With photos, tour hours and a reply to every review.
c0802: The Knot / WeddingWire storefronts: measure the cost per lead
c0804: Start with the basic listing and move to a paid storefront if the numbers work. Note where every booked couple came from.
c0805: Social media with real weddings and events
c0807: Instagram and Pinterest with real setups and written permission from the couples.
c0810: One or two a year, with the caterer. Bring the brochure and a way to book a venue tour on the spot.
c0814: The venue set up, the caterer serving a tasting and the vendors from your preferred vendor list.
c0817: A guided tour, the brochure and a referral commission agreed in writing. The plan assumes one in ten sales comes through planners and venue marketplaces, at a 15% commission. Marketplaces such as Peerspace can add corporate and private events.
c0819: These events fill the winter and the weekdays: corporate retreats, holiday parties, showers, milestone birthdays and rehearsal dinners.
c0822: Use the pricing calculator in this pack: peak, shoulder and off-peak seasons, Saturday vs Friday, Sunday and weekdays, guest minimums and add-ons.
c0823: Pricing guide / wedding brochure and corporate deck
c0824: What the venue rental includes, what the caterer provides, indicative rates, payment schedule and terms.
c0825: Venue rental agreement with a retainer and cancellation table, reviewed by an attorney
c0827: Start from the template in this pack and have an attorney in your state review it. Keep the retainer and the cancellation table reasonable and mutual: if you keep what the couple paid when they cancel, agree the same terms for when you cancel.
c0828: Venue management software and date calendar
c0829: One calendar for tours, blocked dates, retainers and pending payments.
c0835: A quote from the calculator, valid for a set period, with what is included and what is not.
c0838: Every payment, retainer included, gets a receipt or invoice, with sales tax if your state taxes the venue rental fee.
c0839: Signing at bridal shows or off-site
c0840: If you sign couples at bridal shows or off-site, ask your attorney whether the FTC Cooling-Off Rule or your state's home-solicitation law applies; many venues give a short cancellation window for show-floor signings anyway.
c0841: Governing law clause reviewed by your attorney
c0842: The contract should say which state's law governs and where disputes are heard. Consumer rules differ by state, so have your attorney review the clause.
c0846: The menu isn't final without it. The caterer charges for the tasting or credits it, according to its own contract.
c0850: In writing, with the allergies and intolerances of each table. It's the basis for the caterer commission and for the day-of staffing.
c0853: Tent ready and couples informed. Sparklers, fireworks and open flames can be banned during fire danger periods: check with your county and fire marshal.
c0857: Never more guests than your certificate of occupancy allows. Keep signage in place and exits clear.
c0859: Outdoor music until the curfew in your permit. Move the last dance inside and watch the sound meter. Point the speakers away from neighbors.
c0860: Walkthrough before guests arrive: clear exits, restrooms and the COIs of the day's vendors
c0861: Check that exits are clear, restrooms are ready and every vendor working today has sent a COI.
c0864: End of the event and next day
c0865: Photograph the condition of the venue afterward. Any damage is deducted from the security deposit as the contract says, itemized, and the refundable balance is returned.
c0866: Monthly commission statement with the caterer
c0868: Reconcile the signed headcount of each event with the caterer's statement, then invoice the commission.
c0871: Ask the couple for a review and the photographer for photos, with permission to publish them.
c0872: Quarterly review: occupancy, commission and cash
c0873: Events held vs the plan, revenue per guest, commission collected and cash balance vs the "12-Month Cash Flow" sheet.
